# Vaccination

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Basics of infectious diseases > Vaccination*

[Original Article Link](/library/_m05Rg)

---

## Summary

Vaccination is a very effective measure for providing <u>immunity</u> to many infectious diseases. The discovery of vaccines played a central part in the eradication of <u>smallpox</u> and helped significantly reduce the <u>incidence</u> of potentially severe diseases such as <u>poliomyelitis</u> and <u>measles</u>. <u>Live vaccines</u> (attenuated, i.e., noninfective pathogens), <u>inactivated vaccines</u> (subunits or complete pathogens), <u>viral vector vaccines</u>, and <u>nucleic acid</u> vaccines (<u>DNA</u>, <u>RNA</u>, <u>mRNA</u>, or viral replicons) are used to achieve <u>active immunization</u>, which enables the host's <u>immune system</u> to build up a sustained <u>immune response</u> to specific pathogens. The <u>immune response</u> may be measured and quantified by assessing the <u>antibody</u> <u>titer</u>. In the event of potential disease (e.g., after exposure to high-risk pathogens), if the <u>immune system</u> is unable to produce sufficient <u>antibodies</u> fast enough, <u>passive immunization</u> can offer immediate short-term protection via direct injection of pooled <u>antibodies</u> for many conditions. Modern vaccines are usually well-tolerated, and <u>adverse events</u> are rare. However, the intervals between vaccine administration and possible contraindications must be considered. <u>Vaccine hesitancy</u> is an ambivalence or resistance toward receiving vaccination, which may influence the uptake of vaccinations. <u>Vaccine hesitancy</u> can be addressed by empathetically addressing patients' vaccine-related concerns and using <u>motivational interviewing</u> techniques.




For <u>ACIP</u> vaccination recommendations, see “<u>Immunization schedule</u>.”

---

## Definitions

* Vaccine

* A product (e.g., dead or weakened organism) that provides <u>immunity</u> from a disease

* May be administered through injection, orally, or nasally

* Vaccination: administration of a vaccine that induces an active immune reaction in form of cellular and/or <u>humoral response</u>, providing <u>immunity</u> against a <u>pathogen</u>

* Immunization

* The process by which a person becomes protected from a disease

* Vaccines and recovering from some infections cause <u>immunization</u>.





References:[[1]](/library/M2aMRP)

---

## Passive immunization

* Mechanism of action

* Injection of preformed <u>antibodies</u> induces a rapid <u>humoral response</u> against a specific <u>pathogen</u>

* Provides only temporary protection, as <u>antibodies</u> have a <u>half-life</u> of ∼ 3 weeks and their <u>titers</u> decrease over time.

* Examples

* <u>Antitoxins</u>

* Humanized <u>monoclonal antibodies</u>

* Maternal <u>immunoglobulins</u> that are transmitted via <u>breast milk</u> (<u>IgA</u>) or cross the <u>placenta</u> (<u>IgG</u>) to provide <u>passive immunity</u>

* <u>Intravenous immunoglobulins</u> to provide temporary <u>passive immunity</u> to a specific <u>pathogen</u> (e.g., <u>CMV</u>)

* Indications

* Acute, post-exposure elimination of a <u>pathogen</u>

* <u>Viruses</u>: <u>rubella</u>, <u>rabies</u>, <u>hepatitis B</u>

* Toxins: <u>tetanus</u>, botulinum, <u>diphtheria</u>

* <u>Rhesus incompatibility</u> prevention

* Application: Vaccines are available for intramuscular as well as for intravenous injection .

* Combination

* <u>Simultaneous vaccination</u>

* Two different passive vaccines may be administered simultaneously.

* An inactivated active and a <u>passive vaccine</u> may be administered simultaneously (e.g., in acute <u>hepatitis A</u>, <u>hepatitis B</u>, <u>rabies</u>, or <u>tetanus</u> infection). [[4]](/library/0eYexL)

* After <u>transfusion</u> of certain <u>blood products</u> and/or <u>immunoglobulin</u> therapy, <u>live vaccines</u> should be delayed depending on the estimated amount of <u>IgG</u> in the <u>transfusion</u>.  [[5]](/library/l2Wv3k0)[[6]](/library/Ef18LT0)





> [!NOTE]
> “<u>Passive immunization</u> Helps Beat The Disease Rapidly:” HBV, Botulinum, Tetanus, Diphtheria, and Rabies are indications for <u>passive immunization</u>.

---

## Active immunization

* General information

* In active immunity, the body's <u>immune system</u> reacts to the presence of <u>antigens</u> by producing <u>antibodies</u>.

* In general, a combination of different <u>active vaccinations</u> is possible.

* Slow onset, but <u>immunity</u> usually lasts for years or even a lifetime.

* Besides vaccines and toxoids, natural infections lead to <u>active immunization</u> as well.

* Classification 

* <u>Live attenuated vaccines</u>

* <u>Inactivated vaccines</u>

* <u>Whole vaccines</u>

* <u>Subunit vaccines</u>

* Protein-based (subunit and <u>toxoid vaccines</u>)

* <u>Polysaccharide</u>-based

* <u>Viral vector vaccines</u>

* <u>Nucleic acid</u> vaccines (<u>DNA</u>, <u>RNA</u>, <u>mRNA</u>, or viral replicons)





Current vaccination recommendations for the US can be found in the “<u>Immunization schedule</u>.”




![Vaccine types](media/v93stk0ivon2c0f3n40d0wdd.jpg)

## Live attenuated vaccines

* Definition: Modified functioning <u>virus</u> or bacterium that can replicate in the patient's body but does not cause disease.

* Mechanism of action

* Similar to an infection with a “wild” <u>pathogen</u> and  induces a cellular and <u>humoral immune response</u>.

* Specific <u>B-cells</u> against an <u>antigen</u> are formed, which induces a potent, lifelong <u>immune response</u>

* Administration

* Oral vaccine or subcutaneous/intramuscular injection in children > 12 months

* Not indicated in children < 9 months;   (the <u>rotavirus vaccine</u> is an exception, which is first given at 6 weeks of age)

* Second dose usually recommended to “catch” nonresponders (not as a boost)

* Multiple <u>live vaccines</u> can be given simultaneously, but if given at different times they should be at least 4 weeks apart to avoid possible interference.

* May be administered simultaneously with <u>inactivated vaccines</u>

* Available vaccines

* <u>MMR</u>: prevents <u>measles</u>, <u>mumps</u> and <u>rubella</u> infections

* <u>Varicella</u>: against <u>varicella-zoster virus</u> (<u>VZV</u>)

* Zoster: prevents reactivation of latent <u>VZV</u> (i.e., <u>shingles</u>)

* <u>Yellow fever</u>

* <u>Rotavirus</u>

* <u>Influenza</u> (intranasal)

* <u>Smallpox</u>

* <u>Adenovirus</u>

* Oral <u>polio</u>, Sabin (no longer available in the US)

* <u>BCG</u>

* <u>Typhoid</u> (oral, Ty21a)

* Special considerations

* Very rarely, <u>live attenuated vaccines</u> may become <u>virulent</u> again and are thus often contraindicated in <u>immunodeficient</u> individuals and pregnant women .

* <u>HIV</u>-positive individuals can be vaccinated with <u>live attenuated vaccines</u> (e.g., <u>MMR</u> and <u>varicella</u>) if their <u>CD4</u> cell count is â¥ 200/mmÂ³.

* <u>Adenovirus</u> vaccine is given in its nonattenuated form to military recruits.





> [!NOTE]
> “TYler And Paul Burnt their INFamous ROasted YELLOW-RUBy CHICKEN MEAt Very MUch”: TYphoid, Adenovirus, Polio, BCG, INFluenza, ROtavirus, YELLOW <u>fever</u>, RUBella, CHICKENpox, MEAsles, Varicella, and MUmps are <u>live attenuated vaccines</u>.

## Viral vector vaccines

* Definition: an unrelated <u>virus</u> (e.g., <u>adenovirus</u>, <u>vesicular</u> <u>stomatitis</u> <u>virus</u>, <u>influenza virus</u>) is modified to be used as a nonpathogenic <u>vector</u> that delivers <u>genetic code</u> to cells containing instructions for the production of the desired <u>antigen</u>. [[11]](/library/iQcJDX0)

* Mechanism of action  

* There are two types of <u>viral vector vaccines</u>: replicating and nonreplicating

* Nonreplicating <u>vector</u> vaccines: enter the cells and induce the production of <u>vaccine antigens</u>, but cannot produce new viral particles

* Replicating <u>vector</u> vaccines

* Enter the cells, inducing the production of new viral particles

* New viral particles go on to infect other host cells, leading to the production of further viral and <u>vaccine antigens</u>

* Induce both <u>humoral</u> and cellular <u>immune responses</u>

* Administration: usually injected intramuscularly, but can also be administered intranasally, intradermally, and orally

* Available vaccines

* <u>Ebola virus</u> vaccine (rVSV-ZEBOV; Ervebo)

* <u>COVID-19 vaccine</u> (Janssen <u>COVID-19 vaccine</u>, Vaxzevria, Sputnik V vaccine)

* Special considerations

* Preexisting <u>immunity</u> to the <u>virus</u> that serves as the <u>vector</u> may affect the <u>effectiveness</u> of a vaccine.  [[12]](/library/6P1jfS0)

* Less strict storage and handling conditions than <u>nucleic acid</u> vaccines

* Viral <u>vectors</u> are genetically stable and lack a <u>viral genome</u> and nonstructural <u>proteins</u>. Therefore, they do not interact or integrate into the host's <u>DNA</u> and are nonpathogenic.





![Mechanism of action of viral vector-based COVID-19 vaccines](media/vhbhlkyh8yk71lznolxqbpak.jpg)

Mechanism of action of viral vector-based COVID-19 vaccines

## Nucleic acid vaccines

### RNA vaccines [[13]](/library/hQccDX0)[[14]](/library/3QcSDX0)




* Definition: a vaccine based on <u>mRNA</u> that delivers <u>genetic code</u> containing instructions for the production of the desired <u>antigen</u> to cells

* Mechanism of action  

* Two types of <u>mRNA vaccines</u>: nonreplicating and self-amplifying

* Nonreplicating <u>mRNA vaccines</u>: contain the sequence of the desired <u>antigen</u> and the 5′ and 3′ untranslated regions

* Self-amplifying <u>mRNA vaccines</u>: contain the sequence of the desired <u>antigen</u> and the viral replication machinery (e.g., <u>RNA polymerase</u>) that enables intracellular <u>RNA</u> amplification

* Both types induce <u>humoral</u> as well as cellular <u>immune responses</u>.

* Administration

* Injected intramuscularly or intradermally

* Require multiple doses

* Available vaccines: <u>COVID-19 vaccines</u> (e.g., <u>Comirnaty</u>, <u>Spikevax</u>) contain modified <u>mRNA</u> embedded in lipid nanoparticles that encodes for the spike protein <u>mRNA</u> sequence of <u>SARS-CoV-2</u>

* Special considerations

* <u>mRNA</u> is a nonintegrating platform that is degraded by normal cellular processes. Due to its transitory nature, <u>mRNA</u> does not interact or integrate into the <u>DNA</u> and bears no risk of insertional mutagenesis. (e.g., <u>COVID-19 vaccines</u> are safe to use during <u>pregnancy</u>)

* There is no potential risk of infection as <u>mRNA</u> is nonpathogenic.

* Require strict cold-chain

* Different techniques can be used to deliver the vaccine (e.g., injection of naked <u>mRNA</u> or encapsulated within nanoparticles or polyplex)





![Mechanism of action of mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines](media/nekwrd3z86yqu4mmr8yuhbf8.jpg)

Mechanism of action of mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines




### DNA vaccines [[15]](/library/RQclDX0)




* Definition: A specific <u>antigen</u>-coding <u>DNA</u> sequence is introduced using a genetically engineered <u>plasmid</u> to induce <u>endogenous</u> <u>antigen</u> production in the host.

* Mechanism of action

* After entering the cells, the <u>vaccine antigen</u> is expressed from the <u>DNA</u> construct.

* Induce both <u>humoral</u> and cellular <u>immune responses</u>

* Administration

* Intramuscularly or intradermally

* Require multiple doses

* Available vaccines: No <u>DNA vaccines</u> have been approved for human use in the United States.

* Special considerations

* Potential advantages observed in animal models are improved vaccine stability and the use of nonpathogenic agents.

* In order to properly deliver the vaccine and ensure cellular uptake, injection needs to be followed by <u>electroporation</u>.

## Adverse effects of vaccination

### Common adverse effects [[16]](/library/L2awRP)[[17]](/library/1eY2BL)[[18]](/library/WeYPBL)




* Affects ∼ 1/3

* Usually begin within the first 48–72 hours after administration and last 1–2 days

* Symptoms

* Local swelling, redness, and <u>pain</u> at the injection site

* Low-grade <u>fever</u> (postvaccination fever)

* <u>Headaches</u>

* Fatigue

* <u>Flu-like</u> symptoms

* <u>Live attenuated vaccine</u>: can cause mild form of the disease, usually appearing within 1–3 weeks of administration   :usually caused by replication of the attenuated vaccine strain





### Rare adverse effects [[16]](/library/L2awRP)[[17]](/library/1eY2BL)[[18]](/library/WeYPBL)




* Cardiovascular complications: observed in young men who received <u>mRNA vaccines</u> (<u>COVID-19 vaccines</u>) [[19]](/library/pP1LfS0)

* <u>Pericarditis</u>

* <u>Myocarditis</u>

* <u>Myocardial</u> <u>ischemia</u>

* Serious <u>allergic reaction</u> (generally < 1 per million doses)

* <u>Live attenuated vaccine</u>: attenuated course of the disease following <u>immunization</u> (e.g., vaccine-related <u>measles</u>)

* Vaccine injury (∼ 1/1,000,000): permanent injury from a vaccination or a vaccine-related complication (e.g., <u>encephalopathy</u>, <u>seizures</u>, <u>brachial neuritis</u>)





> [!TIP]
> There is no link between <u>autism</u> and vaccines or their ingredients. [[20]](/library/sVXtDC)[[21]](/library/62ajiP)

---

## Contraindications for vaccination

### Precautions




* General precautions

* A precaution is a condition in the recipient that might increase the risk for serious <u>adverse reactions</u> or interfere with a vaccine's ability to produce <u>immunity</u>.

* Generally, vaccination should be deferred when a precaution is present, except when the benefits of protection outweigh the risks.

* Acute moderate or severe illness (with or without <u>fever</u>)

* Special precautions

* <u>Rotavirus vaccine</u>: uncorrected <u>GI tract</u> <u>malformation</u> (e.g., <u>Meckel's diverticulum</u>)

* <u>Egg protein-containing vaccines</u>: <u>allergic reactions</u> other than <u>urticaria</u> (e.g., <u>angioedema</u>, <u>bronchospasm</u>) to egg products

* <u>Pertussis vaccine</u>: progressive or unstable neurologic disorders (e.g., uncontrolled <u>epilepsy</u>, <u>infantile spasms</u>, progressive <u>encephalopathy</u>)  [[22]](/library/eVaxtj)

* <u>Tetanus toxoid</u>-containing vaccines

* Development of <u>Guillain-Barré syndrome</u> within 6 weeks of a previous dose

* <u>Arthus reaction</u> after a previous dose  [[22]](/library/eVaxtj)





### Contraindications [[23]](/library/Yq0nCS)




* General contraindications

* Vaccines are generally contraindicated in recipients with conditions that increase the risk for severe vaccine reactions or in whom the vaccine may exacerbate the condition.

* Previous severe <u>adverse reactions</u> (e.g., <u>anaphylaxis</u>)

* Severe <u>adverse reactions</u> to a vaccine component (e.g., egg protein in <u>yellow fever vaccine</u>, <u>yeast</u> in <u>hepatitis B vaccine</u>)

* Contraindications to live vaccines

* <u>Rotavirus vaccine</u>

* <u>Severe combined immunodeficiency</u> (<u>SCID</u>)

* History of <u>intussusception</u>  [[24]](/library/J2asiP)

* <u>Pertussis</u> vaccines: risk of <u>encephalopathy</u> (e.g., prolonged <u>seizures</u>, decreased <u>level of consciousness</u>, <u>coma</u>) within 7 days following a previous dose

* Live, attenuated <u>virus</u> vaccinations  [[22]](/library/eVaxtj)

* Pregnant individuals

* <u>Immunodeficient</u> individuals (e.g., individuals receiving <u>chemotherapy</u> or long-term <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u>, individuals with <u>congenital immunodeficiencies</u>, patients with <u>HIV</u> and severe <u>immunocompromise</u>)

* Individuals receiving IVIG therapy (e.g., for <u>Kawasaki disease</u>)

* False contraindications  [[25]](/library/bsXHtz)[[26]](/library/XsX9tz)

* <u>Fever</u> within 48 hours

* Current or recent mild illness (e.g., <u>rhinorrhea</u>, <u>otitis media</u>, mild <u>diarrhea</u>)

* Current or recent <u>antibiotic therapy</u> (exception is oral live <u>typhoid vaccine</u> )

* Current or recent low-dose and/or short-term <u>steroid</u> use (i.e., < 2 mg/kg/day or < 20 mg/day, < 14 days)

* Previous mild or moderate localized cutaneous reaction (e.g., swelling, redness, soreness) following any vaccination

* <u>Preterm infants</u>

* Should be immunized according to chronological age, not <u>gestational age</u>

* The exception is the <u>hepatitis B vaccine</u>: vaccination should be delayed by a month or until <u>hospital discharge</u> for <u>infants</u> weighing < 2 kg born to <u>HBsAg</u>-negative mothers.

* Adjustment according to weight: no dose adjustment is needed





> [!TIP]
> All children should be immunized with the standard doses of vaccines according to their chronological age; doses should not be adjusted to weight or height.

---

## Special patient groups

<u>Immunizations during pregnancy</u>, <u>vaccinations in preterm infants</u>, and <u>vaccinations in individuals with HIV</u> are detailed in the “<u>Immunization schedule</u>” article.

## Vaccine hesitancy

### Overview [[27]](/library/Xbd9Ho0)[[28]](/library/W9WPmn0)




* <u>Vaccine hesitancy</u> is a state of feeling ambivalent about or resistant to receiving vaccinations.

* <u>Vaccine hesitancy</u> may lead to:

* Delay of vaccinations

* Cautious acceptance of vaccinations

* Refusal of some or all vaccinations

* Individuals may express <u>vaccine hesitancy</u> for themselves and/or their children.





### Approach [[27]](/library/Xbd9Ho0)[[29]](/library/0wWehn0)[[30]](/library/DwW1On0)




Follow the <u>key principles of communication and counseling</u> with all patients.




* Presume individuals have no <u>vaccine hesitancy</u>, and make a strong recommendation for vaccination.

* If the individual declines, inquire sensitively about and address vaccine-related concerns.

* If the individual continues to express hesitancy:

* Use <u>motivational interviewing</u> techniques to facilitate further discussion.

* Continue to definitively recommend adherence to the standard <u>immunization schedule</u>.

* Consider sharing personal or family experience with vaccines.

* If the individual refuses vaccination:

* Affirm their <u>autonomy</u>.

* Document the individual's decision.   [[31]](/library/XwW9hn0)

* Continue to build trust over time and revisit the conversation at a later date.

* Consider dismissal of the patient from the practice only after careful consideration of implications for patient's health and care.  [[27]](/library/Xbd9Ho0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Vaccine hesitancy</u> is a complex issue with no single effective solution. Engage with the individual regarding their concerns and social and cultural context. [[32]](/library/1wW23n0)




> [!TIP]
> Discuss vaccines with the use of evidence-based information, e.g., vaccine information statements for individual vaccines, and leaflets and infographics provided by the American Academy of <u>Pediatrics</u> and <u>CDC</u>. See “Tips and links.”




### Vaccine-related concerns [[27]](/library/Xbd9Ho0)[[33]](/library/iedJAK0)[[34]](/library/jed_AK0)

| Concern |  | <u>Patient counseling</u> topics and strategies |
| <br><u>Simultaneous vaccination</u>  [[35]](/library/SDWydn0)<br> |  | <br><br>* Vaccines stimulate the <u>immune system</u> to perform its intended function.<br><br>* There are no alternative recommended schedules.<br><br>* Delaying or spacing out vaccinations:<br><br>* Places individuals at risk of disease when they are most vulnerable<br><br>* Increases the number of potentially painful injections an individual receives<br><br><br> |
| <br>Safety of vaccine components [[36]](/library/3bdSto0)[[37]](/library/QDWuVn0)<br> |  | <br><br>* Each vaccine component  serves a specific purpose.<br><br>* <u>Influenza vaccines</u> that don't contain thimerosal (a <u>mercury</u>-based preservative) are available.  [[38]](/library/3DWSVn0)<br><br>* Standard vaccine development is a rigorous process.   [[27]](/library/Xbd9Ho0)[[39]](/library/1bd2so0)[[40]](/library/cbdaso0)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Adverse effects of vaccination</u> |  | <br><br>* Most reactions are local and mild.<br><br>* Systemic symptoms (e.g., <u>postvaccination fever</u>) are normal <u>immune responses</u>.<br><br>* Provide <u>anticipatory guidance</u> about potential vaccine-specific adverse effects.<br><br>* Postvaccination <u>syncope</u> after the <u>HPV vaccine</u>, <u>meningococcal conjugate vaccine</u> 4 (MCV4), or <u>Tdap vaccine</u>  [[41]](/library/ADWRSn0)<br><br>* Increased risk of <u>febrile seizures</u> following the <u>measles</u>, <u>mumps</u>, <u>rubella</u>, <u>varicella</u> (<u>MMRV</u>) vaccine  [[42]](/library/551ikh0)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Fear and <u>pain</u> of needles [[27]](/library/Xbd9Ho0)[[43]](/library/4EW3DM0)<br> |  | <br><br>* Prior to injection<br><br>* Topical <u>anesthetics</u>  [[44]](/library/8Q1OBg0)<br><br>* Rubbing the <u>skin</u><br><br>* During injection<br><br>* Distractions (e.g., deep breathing exercises, toys for children)<br><br>* Holding young patients upright<br><br>* Administering vaccine quickly, without <u>aspirating</u><br><br>* Consider giving the most painful vaccine (e.g., <u>MMR</u>, <u>HPV</u>) last. [[45]](/library/kedm_K0)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Autism</u> |  | <br>* Multiple studies have shown that there is no link between <u>autism</u> and vaccinations. [[46]](/library/DDW1gn0)<br><br> |
| Natural <u>immunity</u> is preferable to vaccination |  | <br><br>* Vaccination is much safer than being infected with a <u>vaccine-preventable disease</u>.<br><br>* <u>Passive immunity</u> from <u>breastfeeding</u> provides less disease protection than vaccines, and it fades over 6–12 months. [[47]](/library/HwWK4n0)<br><br><br> |
| Vaccine <u>efficacy</u> |  | <br>* Vaccination reduces <u>vaccine-preventable diseases</u> and associated deaths. [[48]](/library/awWQhn0)[[49]](/library/fedkyK0)<br><br> |
| Getting illness from vaccines |  | <br><br>* The pathogens in <u>inactivated vaccines</u> are not living and cannot cause disease.<br><br>* In immunocompetent individuals, <u>live vaccines</u> may rarely cause mild disease.<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Unapproved delayed or alternate <u>immunization schedules</u> put individuals at risk for <u>vaccine-preventable conditions</u> and complications. [[27]](/library/Xbd9Ho0)




> [!WARNING]
> Refusal of vaccines may lead to exclusion from school. Check with local state and health departments. [[50]](/library/YwWnhn0)
